planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions shallowly in fall into heavier, moisture-retentive soil than other Pacific Coast iris relatives tolerate, matching its seasonally wet coastal prairie habitat.

directions: Native to seasonally wet coastal prairies and grassy bluffs from Sonoma County south through the Santa Cruz Mountains and Monterey Peninsula, coast iris grows in heavier, moisture-retentive clay soils that would rot most of its Pacific Coast iris relatives. Its pale lavender-blue to soft violet flowers are among the largest of any California native iris, with darker purple veining radiating across broad falls and an unusually long floral tube that gives the species its name. Unlike the shade-loving woodland Pacific Coast irises, it thrives in open, full-sun grassland alongside native bunchgrasses and still requires a dry summer dormancy despite its wetter winter and spring habitat. Use it in a naturalistic coastal meadow planting or restored prairie rather than a conventional border, since it resents summer irrigation once established.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions shallowly in fall in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun; this maritime species tolerates salt spray and wind that would damage most garden perennials.

directions: Restricted to rocky headlands and gravelly beaches of the Gulf of St. Lawrence and the Atlantic coast of Quebec, the Maritime Provinces, and Down East Maine, this compact iris grows almost within reach of salt spray. It is closely allied to the more widespread Iris setosa of Alaska and the Pacific Northwest and is sometimes treated as a variety of that species, but its shorter stature, denser clumping habit, and differing chromosome count support its recognition as a distinct species by USDA PLANTS and several regional floras. Flowers are violet-blue with the same bristle-reduced standards typical of the setosa group, held just above tufted, wind-battered foliage in late spring to early summer. Give it full sun, sharp drainage, and an exposed site; it is remarkably tolerant of poor, gravelly soil and coastal wind but performs poorly in hot, humid inland gardens.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions shallowly in fall into fast-draining soil in an open, sunny coastal-prairie setting, then withhold summer water entirely once established.

directions: Endemic to a narrow stretch of coastal prairie and serpentine grassland near Port Orford and Cape Blanco in Curry County, Oregon, Gorman's iris is treated by most modern floras as a distinct subspecies of the widespread Oregon iris (Iris tenax). It is immediately distinguishable from typical Iris tenax by its flower color, a pale cream to soft butter-yellow rather than the rose-purple to lavender-blue typical of the species elsewhere in its range. Like its parent species it forms tufted clumps of narrow, grass-like foliage that go dormant after a spring bloom and a dry summer rest, and it is best grown in an open, unirrigated meadow planting rather than a conventionally watered border. Because its native range is so restricted, source plants only from nurseries propagating from cultivated stock rather than wild-collected material.
